awd_titl_txt: Geometry and Integrability of Random Processes
awd_abstract_narration:
Two major goals of probability theory are to address the question of how large complex systems work and to identify the geometry of their evolution. Probabilistic models are widespread in fields like biology, statistical physics, quantum mechanics, and machine learning. Examples include models of cancer growth, spread of disease in population, governing principles of subatomic particles, black holes, neural networks, etc. The purpose of this project is to understand the geometry and intrinsic properties of a string of models that are representatives of these examples. The project aims to resolve open questions in those fields based on tools that the investigator has developed. 

Domino tilings, random matrices, and stochastic six vertex models are areas of intense interest in the field of statistical physics, while Liouville conformal field theory (LCFT) and theory of optimal transport have gained immense attention in the fields of quantum mechanics and machine learning. This project revolves around questions in those areas and aims to acquire new insights about their geometry and integrability. In particular, this project plans to: (1) find laws of iterated logarithms and fractal dimension of models in the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) universality class including the KPZ fixed point, edge spectrum of random matrices, and domino tilings; (2) build a unified framework for studying the moment formulas of interacting particle systems and vertex models including the stochastic six vertex model; (3) rigorously prove modular transformation properties of conformal blocks of LCFT and partition functions from gauge theory; and (4) study the convergence of entropically regularized optimal transport to optimal transport when the regularization vanishes. By intermingling ideas from various fields including geometry of polymers, representation theory, Riemann-Hilbert techniques, quantum groups, and convex geometry, the investigator aims to resolve questions that were hard to tackle with other methods.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

PROJECT OUTCOMES REPORT NSF Award: Geometry and Integrability of Random Processes

OVERVIEW: This project advanced our mathematical understanding of random phenomena that appear throughout nature and technology—from how coffee stains form to how traffic flows on highways, and from the spread of infections to the growth of bacterial colonies. These seemingly unrelated phenomena share common mathematical structures that this research helped reveal.

MAJOR ACHIEVEMENTS: 

1. FRACTAL GEOMETRY OF RANDOM GROWTH: One of the project's central achievements was developing a comprehensive mathematical framework for understanding the geometric properties of random growth processes. Think of how a droplet spreads on paper or how a bacterial colony grows—these processes create intricate, rough boundaries. The PI with his collaborators established foundational tools to measure and predict the "roughness" of these boundaries using fractal geometry. This work focused on singular stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), including the famous Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation, which describes how random surfaces grow over time, and the parabolic Anderson model, which describes how randomness affects heat diffusion. These equations are "singular" because they involve extreme random fluctuations that make them mathematically challenging to analyze. The framework developed in this project lays groundwork for future investigations of even more complex systems, including critical stochastic heat flow, turbulent fluid dynamics (Navier-Stokes equations), and quantum field theories like stochastic Yang-Mills equations. These advances will enable scientists and engineers to better predict and control random phenomena in diverse applications.

2. INTERACTING PARTICLE SYSTEMS AND SPEED PROCESSES: The project solved a longstanding open problem concerning the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP), a fundamental model for studying how particles move when they interact—imagine cars on a one-way highway where vehicles cannot pass each other. The PI with his collaborators constructed the "invariant measure" of the ASEP speed process, which describes the long-term statistical behavior of particle velocities. This achievement involved developing sophisticated mathematical techniques connecting random matrix theory with orthogonal polynomials and applying powerful analytical tools called Riemann-Hilbert methods. The team is completing a comprehensive monograph on moderate deviation asymptotics for stochastic six-vertex models, which will provide a unified framework for understanding rare events in these systems. These results have implications for understanding traffic flow, queueing systems, and molecular transport in biological cells.

3. CONFORMAL FIELD THEORY AND QUANTUM GRAVITY: The project made breakthrough contributions to Liouville quantum gravity, a mathematical theory describing random geometric surfaces that appears in string theory and statistical physics. The PI with his collaborators proved the Zamolodchikov conjecture for the semiclassical limit of Liouville conformal field theory—a fundamental result that had remained open for decades. Additionally, the team established fusion relations for probabilistic conformal blocks, which represent a quantitative manifestation of "S-duality" in supersymmetric gauge theories. S-duality is a remarkable symmetry in quantum physics that relates theories with weak and strong coupling constants. This work bridges probability theory, quantum field theory, and high-energy physics, providing rigorous mathematical foundations for phenomena previously understood only through physical intuition.

4. OPTIMAL TRANSPORT AND ENTROPIC SELECTION: The project advanced the theory of entropic optimal transport, which addresses the classical problem posed by Gaspard Monge in 1781: how to optimally transport mass from one location to another while minimizing cost. In modern applications, this appears in machine learning, image processing, economics, and logistics. The PI with his collaborators proved an "entropic selection principle" for Monge's optimal transport problem, demonstrating that when multiple optimal transport maps exist, adding entropy regularization naturally selects a unique solution. This result has practical importance because entropy regularization enables efficient computational algorithms (Sinkhorn's algorithm) that are widely used in data science and artificial intelligence applications.

BROADER IMPACTS:  This research trained graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in cutting-edge mathematical techniques at the intersection of probability theory, analysis, and mathematical physics. The methods and results developed have applications across multiple scientific disciplines, from statistical physics to machine learning. The project's outcomes strengthen connections between pure mathematics and applied fields, demonstrating how abstract mathematical theories provide essential tools for understanding real-world phenomena. By establishing rigorous foundations for random processes, this work enables more reliable predictions in applications ranging from materials science to financial mathematics to machine learning algorithms. The research has been disseminated through publications in top-tier mathematical journals, presentations at international conferences, and collaborative workshops, fostering interdisciplinary dialogue and training the next generation of researchers in these vital areas of mathematics.
